title: Pretraining Data Can Be Poisoned through Computational Propaganda
hook: Most pretraining-poisoning research injects fake Wikipedia edits — a toy case next to messy web-scale reality. This paper shows public discussion forums are a real, live vector for attacking LLM pretraining data.
key_points: Prior poisoning research mostly used established, curated sources (like Wikipedia) that don't represent the scale and heterogeneity of real pretraining corpora, and ignored how curation pipelines interact with poisoned data.
Demonstrates that public discussion interfaces (comment sections, forums) are a viable, existing content-injection mechanism for poisoning pretraining data at web scale.
Introduces HalfLife, a method for estimating whether adversarially injected content actually survives web crawling and curation into training data.
Establishes third-party webpage content (not just a site's own primary content) as a realistic attack vector on LLM pretraining.
content_html: Poisoning a language model's pretraining data can plant behaviors that are hard to detect and hard to remove later. But most prior work on this threat used tidy, well-curated sources like Wikipedia to demonstrate it — a setting that doesn't capture the scale or messiness of a real web-scale pretraining corpus, and one that skips over whether standard data-curation pipelines would even let the poisoned content through.
extra_html:
Victoria Graf and colleagues, including researchers from the Allen Institute for AI, show poisoning is feasible well beyond that limited setting, using an existing and very ordinary content-injection mechanism: public discussion interfaces, like comment sections and forums that get swept into web crawls. To check whether such injected content actually makes it into training data after crawling and curation — rather than being filtered out along the way — they introduce HalfLife, a method for estimating adversarial content's survival rate through that pipeline.

Put together, the two contributions make the case that third-party webpage content, not just a site's own primary text, is a realistic and underappreciated vector for attacking LLM pretraining at web scale — and that measuring whether an injection actually survives curation is essential to judging how serious that risk really is. Source: arXiv, arxiv.org/abs/2607.15267.

related.title: Deduplicating Training Data Makes LMs Better
related.hook: Training corpora are full of copies — one 61-word sentence shows up 60,000+ times in C4. Strip the duplicates and models memorize far less and evaluate more honestly.

related.title: The Pile: 800GB of Diverse Text
related.hook: Web text alone leaves gaps. The Pile stitches together 22 curated sources — academic and professional — so a language model picks up knowledge plain web crawls miss.

flashcards.explanation_html: The paper's core demonstration is that content injected through open discussion interfaces can enter web-scale training corpora — a more realistic vector than the Wikipedia-editing setups used in prior poisoning studies.

flashcards.prompt: What is HalfLife, and why does it matter?
flashcards.back_html: A method the authors introduce for estimating whether adversarially injected content actually survives web crawling and data curation into a model's training data — since an injection that gets filtered out never poses a real risk.
